chapterTitle: Interacting with the Substrate Runtime: RPC, API, and UI
aiGenerationNote:

screens.title: Interacting with the Substrate Runtime
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn the practical pathways for talking to a running Substrate node. We begin by explaining Remote Procedure Calls, the low-level JSON-RPC surface a node exposes, and why it matters for queries, subscriptions, and submitting transactions. Then we'll introduce the Polkadot-JS A P I — a JavaScript library that wraps those RPC calls, handles SCALE encoding, and helps you sign and broadcast extrinsics. Finally, you'll see how the Polkadot-JS Apps web UI maps the same primitives into a graphical workflow for account management, chain state inspection, and constructing extrinsics. A quick example will ground the ideas: using the A P I to query an account balance and then submit a transfer. I will also point out common developer mistakes like wrong provider URLs, unsigned transactions, and wrong keyring types so you can troubleshoot quickly. By the end you will understand the flow from UI or code down to RPC calls, and why managing keys and trusted nodes is essential for real deployments.

screens.title: What is JSON-RPC for Substrate nodes?
screens.narratorSegment: JSON-RPC is the lightweight protocol a Substrate node uses to accept requests and return responses across a network boundary. At its simplest, JSON-RPC defines a JSON request that names a method and provides parameters; the node executes the corresponding internal function and returns a JSON result. For Substrate, the node exposes methods for reading storage, submitting extrinsics, and subscribing to events, typically over WebSocket or HTTP. A practical consequence is that every Polkadot-JS A P I call or Polkadot-JS Apps action becomes a JSON-RPC request under the hood. For example, when you ask for an account balance, the RPC call carries the encoded account identifier to the node, which decodes it and returns the stored balance value. A common misconception is that JSON-RPC is the same as application logic — it is not. JSON-RPC is only the transport. Your runtime's storage layout and dispatchable signatures determine what methods exist and how parameters are interpreted. A simple troubleshooting step is to check the node's listening ports, usually 9944 for WebSocket in development, and ensure your client uses the correct endpoint. Think of JSON-RPC as the plumbing: critical for flow, but distinct from the appliances that use it.

keyIdea.title: RPC is transport
keyIdea.text: JSON-RPC carries method names and parameters to a node and returns decoded results; it is the plumbing layer beneath APIs and UIs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › RPC Definition
JSON-RPC in Substrate
A protocol for remote procedure calls: methods, params, and JSON responses.
  • Exposes node methods for storage reads, extrinsic submission, and event subscriptions.
  • Works over WebSocket (commonly port 9944) or HTTP (9933) in development setups.
  • Is independent of runtime logic; it simply transports requests and responses.
Example transport check
If your client can't connect, verify the node process is running and the WS port is reachable, then confirm the provider URL string matches exactly.
Illustrative call flow
Misconception: RPC is not runtime logic. The RPC channel carries the calls; the node's runtime defines how calls are handled and what storage exists.

screens.title: Polkadot-JS API: how it abstracts RPC
screens.narratorSegment: Polkadot-JS A P I is the JavaScript client that saves you from writing raw JSON-RPC messages. Conceptually, it sits above the transport layer and offers a typed, object-oriented interface. When you create an ApiPromise and pass a WsProvider, the library opens a WebSocket, fetches runtime metadata, and builds helpers like api. query and api. tx. The metadata is crucial: it describes pallets, storage items, and dispatchable calls so the A P I can encode parameters and decode responses using SCALE. For example, api. query. system. account(accountId) will construct the correct RPC method, encode the account identifier, send the request, and return a decoded structure with free balance and other fields. The A P I also manages connection lifecycle and can subscribe to updates, so you rarely need to handle raw socket events. A common error is assuming api. tx calls are queries; api. tx builds extrinsics for state changes while api. query reads current storage. Another frequent gotcha is forgetting to await ApiPromise. create before using api. The library also integrates signing helpers through Keyring for easy signAndSend calls. Understanding this layered architecture helps you write reliable scripts and avoid low-level encoding errors.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Polkadot-JS API
What the API does
  • Connects using a provider and retrieves runtime metadata to build typed helpers.
  • Encodes and decodes values using SCALE so you work with readable objects instead of raw bytes.
  • Exposes api.query for reads, api.tx for extrinsics, and subscription helpers for events.
Common mistakes
Trying to use api before ApiPromise.create resolves, or mixing keyring types without realizing the chain expects sr25519.
Code example: connect and query balance
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api'); async function main() { const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944'); const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider }); console.log(`Connected to chain: ${api.genesisHash.toHex()}`); const ALICE = '5GrwvaEF5zXb26Fz9rcQpDWS57CtERHpNehXCPcNoHGKutQY'; const { data: { free: aliceFree } } = await api.query.system.account(ALICE); console.log(`Alice's free balance: ${aliceFree.toHuman()} units`); await api.disconnect(); } main().catch(console.error);
This snippet demonstrates connection, metadata use, and a simple storage query; it is safe to run against a local development node.

screens.title: Constructing and sending a transfer extrinsic
screens.narratorSegment: Sending a transaction — an extrinsic — changes chain state and requires careful steps. First, construct the extrinsic using api. tx.. (... args). For a token transfer, that's api. tx. balances. transfer(recipient, amount). Next, you must sign the extrinsic with a private key belonging to the sender. The Polkadot-JS Keyring helps you load development keys like Alice via addFromUri. Finally, call signAndSend with the keypair. The A P I returns a hash or can provide status updates via a subscription callback that tells you when the transaction is in a block or finalized. A common trap is forgetting to provide enough funds to cover both the transferred amount and fees; another is using an incorrect key type for signing. The code example here constructs a transfer, signs it, and prints the returned hash. When writing production code, replace development URIs with secure key storage and always disconnect the A P I when finished. Think of signAndSend as the atomic step that ties the extrinsic to a cryptographic identity and hands it to the network for inclusion. Constructing and sending a transfer extrinsic means build the extrinsic, sign with a keypair, and broadcast; watch status updates to confirm inclusion and finalization.. In practical terms, create, sign, and broadcast a balances.transfer call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Send Extrinsic
Steps to submit a transaction
  1. Create provider and await ApiPromise.create so metadata is available.
  2. Load signer keypair using Keyring and the correct curve (sr25519 for Substrate).
  3. Build extrinsic with api.tx.balances.transfer(recipient, amount).
  4. Call transfer.signAndSend(signer) and monitor status for inclusion/finalization.
Misconception: signing is optional — it is required for any extrinsic that modifies state and must use the corresponding private key.
Code example: transfer
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider, Keyring } = require('@polkadot/api'); async function main() { const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944'); const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider }); const keyring = new Keyring({ type: 'sr25519' }); const alice = keyring.addFromUri('//Alice'); const bob = '5FHneW46xGXap2Few4HEUSRtfAwPCMzrMyGZvou3S85fWkEZ'; const transfer = api.tx.balances.transfer(bob, 10); const hash = await transfer.signAndSend(alice); console.log('Transfer sent with hash', hash.toHex()); await api.disconnect(); } main().catch(console.error);
This example uses development keys; do not expose real private keys in production code.

screens.title: Common Polkadot-JS API troubleshooting steps
screens.narratorSegment: When a script or UI call fails, systematic troubleshooting saves time. Start with the provider: confirm the WebSocket or HTTP URL is correct and that the node process is listening on the expected port. If you see connection refused, check your node logs and firewall. Next, if you receive signature errors, validate that the Keyring type matches the chain's expected curve (sr25519 is default) and that the keypair is correctly loaded. Log the signing account's address and compare it to the intended sender. For transactions that fail due to balance, confirm the account has enough free balance to cover both the transfer and fees by querying api. query. system. account(address). Another helpful pattern is to add status logging to signAndSend to see inclusion and finalization steps. Finally, remember to disconnect the A P I in long-running scripts to avoid leaked sockets. A common misconception is treating returned hashes as confirmation; the hash confirms broadcast, but you should wait for in-block or finalized statuses to confirm state change. These steps give clear checkpoints to isolate network, signature, and balance problems. Common Polkadot-JS API troubleshooting steps means check provider connectivity, keyring and signing setup, account balances, and transaction lifecycle statuses to pinpoint failures.. In practical terms, diagnose connection, signing, and insufficient funds issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Troubleshooting
Step-by-step checks
1. Provider: Verify the WsProvider URL and node listening port (default 9944 for WS in dev).
2. Keyring and signing: Ensure Keyring type is sr25519 and keypair is loaded; log its address.
3. Balance: Query system.account to confirm free balance covers transfer plus fees.
4. Transaction lifecycle: Use signAndSend's callback to observe in-block and finalized statuses.
Quick diagnostic commands
Use small scripts to print connection status and account free balance. Logging the returned status objects from signAndSend often reveals whether a transaction was included or merely broadcast.
Pro-tip: Treat hash as broadcast receipt; wait for in-block or finalized events to confirm state changes.

screens.title: Polkadot-JS Apps: a visual interface
screens.narratorSegment: Polkadot-JS Apps is a browser-based developer UI that connects to a Substrate node and exposes developer tools for inspecting the runtime. It allows you to manage accounts, view storage items and constants, construct and sign extrinsics, and monitor events in real time. For developers building or testing pallets, the Chain State explorer is invaluable: it exposes every storage entry that your runtime metadata advertises, letting you query maps and complex types without writing code. The Extrinsics interface lets you select a pallet and call a dispatchable, supply parameters, and sign immediately with a browser-managed key or extension. Using the UI is an effective way to sanity-check the behavior of newly added pallet functions before wiring them into an application. A common misconception is that the UI can do things the runtime cannot; in reality, the UI simply packages the same RPC calls and signs transactions on behalf of the user. When debugging, switch the Apps network endpoint to your local node and recreate the steps your script performs to compare outputs and events. This gives a fast feedback loop for development.

keyIdea.title: UI as a debugger
keyIdea.text: Polkadot-JS Apps mirrors API capabilities in a human-friendly workspace for exploring metadata, calling extrinsics, and monitoring events.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Polkadot-JS Apps
Developer tools inside Apps
  • Accounts: create, import, and manage keypairs for signing transactions in the browser.
  • Chain State: explore runtime storage, test storage queries, and view decoded values.
  • Extrinsics: build and submit calls to any pallet directly from the UI, with immediate feedback.
  • Events and logs: monitor emitted runtime events as transactions are executed.
Practical walkthrough
To test a new pallet, switch the network endpoint to your local node, open Developer → Chain state to read your storage map, then Developer → Extrinsics to call the dispatchable and observe the generated event.
Analogy: Polkadot-JS Apps is like a database admin UI for your runtime — it queries, updates, and shows a live event log without writing code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Activity
Activity checklist
  1. Start your node locally in development mode.
  2. Create a script that connects with WsProvider and ApiPromise.create.
  3. Load Alice with Keyring and query api.query.<pallet>.accountCounters(alice.address).
  4. Call api.tx.<pallet>.incrementCounter().signAndSend(alice) and wait for finalization.
  5. Re-query to confirm the counter incremented.
Expected result: Alice's counter increases by one after the transaction is included and finalized.
Starter code (interact.js)
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider, Keyring } = require('@polkadot/api'); async function main() { const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944'); const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider }); const keyring = new Keyring({ type: 'sr25519' }); const alice = keyring.addFromUri('//Alice'); // 1. Query initial counter let aliceCounter = await api.query.templateModule.accountCounters(alice.address); console.log(`Alice's initial counter: ${aliceCounter.toNumber()}`); // 2. Submit increment_counter const incrementTx = api.tx.templateModule.incrementCounter(); const hash = await incrementTx.signAndSend(alice); console.log(`Transaction sent with hash: ${hash.toHex()}`); // 3. Wait and re-query await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 5000)); aliceCounter = await api.query.templateModule.accountCounters(alice.address); console.log(`Alice's new counter: ${aliceCounter.toNumber()}`); await api.disconnect(); } main().catch(console.error);

screens.title: Querying state vs. submitting transactions
screens.narratorSegment: Reading chain state and modifying it are distinct actions with different A P I surfaces. Use api. query when you need a snapshot of stored data — this is a read-only operation that does not change the chain and often returns immediately. For example, api. query. system. account returns account balances and nonce information. Use api. tx when you intend to change state: this constructs an extrinsic that must be signed and sent. For example, api. tx. balances. transfer creates a transfer extrinsic. Subscriptions are a third pattern: when you need to react to on-chain events as they happen, subscribe to api. query. system. events or use subscriptions on specific storage items to get push updates. Subscriptions are more efficient than polling and essential for live UIs that must react to new blocks or transfer events. A misconception is that api. query can notify you of future changes; it cannot unless you subscribe. Also remember an extrinsic broadcast returns a hash but not a guarantee of finalization; use status callbacks to observe inclusion and finality. Choosing the right method matters for UX, resource usage, and correctness.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Query vs Tx
api.query (Read)
Snapshot reads of on-chain storage. No signing required and no state change occurs.
  • Use for balances, storage maps, and constants.
  • Instant and safe to call frequently for debugging; consider rate limits for public RPCs.
api.tx (Write)
Builds extrinsics that mutate state. Requires signing and payment of fees.
  • Use signAndSend to broadcast and monitor lifecycle events.
  • Always verify sender, amount, and parameters before signing.
Key takeaway

Choose query for reads, tx for writes, and subscriptions for real-time notifications; treat hash as broadcast and check status to confirm finalization.

screens.title: Security considerations when interacting with nodes
screens.narratorSegment: Security is central when interacting with a blockchain that holds value. First, private keys must never be exposed in plaintext or committed to version control. The development pattern of addFromUri('//Alice') is for local testing only; in production, use hardware wallets or secure key management systems. Second, be cautious about RPC endpoints: a malicious or compromised node can return incorrect state or censor transactions. Always verify the origin of public RPCs and prefer connecting to nodes you control when testing critical functionality. Third, review transactions before signing: confirm recipient addresses, amounts, and call parameters. Also, recognize the risk of replay or incorrect nonce handling if you reuse keypairs across multiple concurrent scripts. A common misunderstanding is that the A P I or UI prevents mistakes for you — they help but do not guarantee safety. Implement logging, use testnets for staging, and when possible have multi-sig or governance checks on high-value actions. These practices reduce the risk of lost funds or mis-signed extrinsics. In practical terms, protect keys, trust endpoints, and review transactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Observing events and subscriptions
screens.narratorSegment: Subscriptions let your application react to on-chain events without polling. With Polkadot-JS A P I you can subscribe to api. query. system. events to receive a stream of events emitted in each block, or subscribe to specific storage items to get updates when they change. Use event subscriptions to filter for particular pallet events such as transfer events or custom pallet notifications. For instance, when you send incrementCounter, the runtime may emit an event indicating success; subscribing to system events and filtering by section and method gives immediate confirmation when a block includes your extrinsic. Subscriptions are more efficient and provide real-time UX improvements, but they require a stable WebSocket connection and careful handling of reconnection logic. A misconception is assuming events are proof of finality — events emitted in a block indicate execution in that block; you may still want to wait for finalization depending on application guarantees. Subscriptions are ideal for UIs and services that must push updates to users when state changes. Observing events and subscriptions means subscribe to system.events or storage updates to react in real time to transactions and runtime activity instead of polling.. In practical terms, use subscriptions to react to transfers and dispatchable outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Subscriptions
Why subscribe?
  • Receive push updates for events and storage changes.
  • Avoid polling and reduce load on public RPC providers.
  • Support real-time UI notifications and backend processing.
Usage note
Subscribe to api.query.system.events(callback) and filter events by event.section and event.method to react to only the signals you need. Remember to handle reconnection and cleanup to avoid memory leaks.
Misconception: events equal finalization. Events show execution within a block; for guaranteed finality, consider waiting for finalized status.

screens.title: Production practices: connecting, signing, and testing
screens.narratorSegment: Moving from development to production requires deliberate changes. Replace development key URIs with secure signing flows such as hardware wallets or remote signing services. Prefer connecting to trusted node endpoints under your control or to audited public endpoints to reduce risk of data tampering. Add extensive logging around signAndSend and subscription handlers so you can trace transaction lifecycles and handle retries or nonce mismatches. For testing, use a dedicated testnet or local node and reproduce the exact steps your production flow will take. When loading runtime metadata, cache it when appropriate but refresh metadata if you upgrade your runtime to avoid encoding mismatches. Finally, consider rate limits and graceful degradation: public RPC providers may throttle requests, so implement backoff and caching layers to prevent service outages. These practices protect assets and make your integrations robust. A frequent misconception is assuming local success guarantees production safety — staging and secure key handling remain essential steps before going live. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical pathways for talking to a running Substrate node. We begin by explaining Remote Procedure Calls, the low-level JSON-RPC surface a node exposes, and why it matters for queries, subscriptions, and submitting transactions. Then we'll introduce the Polkadot-JS A P I — a JavaScript library that wraps those RPC calls, handles SCALE encoding, and helps you sign and broadcast extrinsics. Finally, you'll see how the Polkadot-JS Apps web UI maps the same primitives into a graphical workflow for account management, chain state inspection, and constructing extrinsics. A quick example will ground the ideas: using the A P I to query an account balance and then submit a transfer. I will also point out common developer mistakes like wrong provider URLs, unsigned transactions, and wrong keyring types so you can troubleshoot quickly. By the end you will understand the flow from UI or code down to RPC calls, and why managing keys and trusted nodes is essential for real deployments.

In this chapter you will gain practical skills that let you move from a running Substrate node to meaningful actions. First, you will understand Remote Procedure Calls: what JSON-RPC is and why nodes expose it for queries, subscriptions, and transaction submission. Second, you will use the Polkadot-JS A P I to connect to a node, query storage, and create or sign extrinsics. Third, you will learn how the Polkadot-JS Apps UI reflects the same operations in a graphical way so you can test pallets without writing code. Finally, you will learn common security pitfalls—key management, provider trust, and transaction review—so you build safely. Each objective includes a small practice cue and a milestone so you know when you've mastered the skill. Learning Objectives means master the three interaction layers: rpc for transport, polkadot-js api for programmatic access, and polkadot-js apps for visual testing and quick debugging.. In practical terms, what you'll be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This second objectives slide focuses on safety and a hands-on activity you will complete. You'll learn why private key handling matters and what makes development keys unsafe for production. You will practice connecting to a local node to avoid untrusted endpoints, and learn checks to verify your WS provider is correct. The hands-on activity asks you to query a custom pallet storage map and submit a dispatchable to increment a counter, then re-query to confirm the change. We'll also list common errors — incorrect provider URL, insufficient balance, and unsigned transactions — and show quick ways to diagnose them. By practicing these steps on a local dev node and using development keys like Alice only in test contexts, you will build confidence and avoid costly mistakes on live networks. Security, Troubleshooting, and Hands-on Goals means practice on a local node, treat development keys as test-only, and always verify provider endpoints and transaction signatures before trusting results.. In practical terms, practical precautions and activity checklist. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

JSON-RPC is the lightweight protocol a Substrate node uses to accept requests and return responses across a network boundary. At its simplest, JSON-RPC defines a JSON request that names a method and provides parameters; the node executes the corresponding internal function and returns a JSON result. For Substrate, the node exposes methods for reading storage, submitting extrinsics, and subscribing to events, typically over WebSocket or HTTP. A practical consequence is that every Polkadot-JS A P I call or Polkadot-JS Apps action becomes a JSON-RPC request under the hood. For example, when you ask for an account balance, the RPC call carries the encoded account identifier to the node, which decodes it and returns the stored balance value. A common misconception is that JSON-RPC is the same as application logic — it is not. JSON-RPC is only the transport. Your runtime's storage layout and dispatchable signatures determine what methods exist and how parameters are interpreted. A simple troubleshooting step is to check the node's listening ports, usually 9944 for WebSocket in development, and ensure your client uses the correct endpoint. Think of JSON-RPC as the plumbing: critical for flow, but distinct from the appliances that use it.

Polkadot-JS A P I is the JavaScript client that saves you from writing raw JSON-RPC messages. Conceptually, it sits above the transport layer and offers a typed, object-oriented interface. When you create an ApiPromise and pass a WsProvider, the library opens a WebSocket, fetches runtime metadata, and builds helpers like api. query and api. tx. The metadata is crucial: it describes pallets, storage items, and dispatchable calls so the A P I can encode parameters and decode responses using SCALE. For example, api. query. system. account(accountId) will construct the correct RPC method, encode the account identifier, send the request, and return a decoded structure with free balance and other fields. The A P I also manages connection lifecycle and can subscribe to updates, so you rarely need to handle raw socket events. A common error is assuming api. tx calls are queries; api. tx builds extrinsics for state changes while api. query reads current storage. Another frequent gotcha is forgetting to await ApiPromise. create before using api. The library also integrates signing helpers through Keyring for easy signAndSend calls. Understanding this layered architecture helps you write reliable scripts and avoid low-level encoding errors.

Sending a transaction — an extrinsic — changes chain state and requires careful steps. First, construct the extrinsic using api. tx.. (... args). For a token transfer, that's api. tx. balances. transfer(recipient, amount). Next, you must sign the extrinsic with a private key belonging to the sender. The Polkadot-JS Keyring helps you load development keys like Alice via addFromUri. Finally, call signAndSend with the keypair. The A P I returns a hash or can provide status updates via a subscription callback that tells you when the transaction is in a block or finalized. A common trap is forgetting to provide enough funds to cover both the transferred amount and fees; another is using an incorrect key type for signing. The code example here constructs a transfer, signs it, and prints the returned hash. When writing production code, replace development URIs with secure key storage and always disconnect the A P I when finished. Think of signAndSend as the atomic step that ties the extrinsic to a cryptographic identity and hands it to the network for inclusion. Constructing and sending a transfer extrinsic means build the extrinsic, sign with a keypair, and broadcast; watch status updates to confirm inclusion and finalization.. In practical terms, create, sign, and broadcast a balances.transfer call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a script or UI call fails, systematic troubleshooting saves time. Start with the provider: confirm the WebSocket or HTTP URL is correct and that the node process is listening on the expected port. If you see connection refused, check your node logs and firewall. Next, if you receive signature errors, validate that the Keyring type matches the chain's expected curve (sr25519 is default) and that the keypair is correctly loaded. Log the signing account's address and compare it to the intended sender. For transactions that fail due to balance, confirm the account has enough free balance to cover both the transfer and fees by querying api. query. system. account(address). Another helpful pattern is to add status logging to signAndSend to see inclusion and finalization steps. Finally, remember to disconnect the A P I in long-running scripts to avoid leaked sockets. A common misconception is treating returned hashes as confirmation; the hash confirms broadcast, but you should wait for in-block or finalized statuses to confirm state change. These steps give clear checkpoints to isolate network, signature, and balance problems. Common Polkadot-JS API troubleshooting steps means check provider connectivity, keyring and signing setup, account balances, and transaction lifecycle statuses to pinpoint failures.. In practical terms, diagnose connection, signing, and insufficient funds issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Polkadot-JS Apps is a browser-based developer UI that connects to a Substrate node and exposes developer tools for inspecting the runtime. It allows you to manage accounts, view storage items and constants, construct and sign extrinsics, and monitor events in real time. For developers building or testing pallets, the Chain State explorer is invaluable: it exposes every storage entry that your runtime metadata advertises, letting you query maps and complex types without writing code. The Extrinsics interface lets you select a pallet and call a dispatchable, supply parameters, and sign immediately with a browser-managed key or extension. Using the UI is an effective way to sanity-check the behavior of newly added pallet functions before wiring them into an application. A common misconception is that the UI can do things the runtime cannot; in reality, the UI simply packages the same RPC calls and signs transactions on behalf of the user. When debugging, switch the Apps network endpoint to your local node and recreate the steps your script performs to compare outputs and events. This gives a fast feedback loop for development.

This hands-on activity walks you through querying a custom pallet storage map and submitting a dispatchable using the Polkadot-JS A P I. Begin with a running local node and a small script that creates a WsProvider and awaits ApiPromise. create. Use Keyring to load Alice's development key and then call api. query.. accountCounters(alice. address) to read the current counter. Reading chain state and modifying it are distinct actions with different A P I surfaces. Use api. query when you need a snapshot of stored data — this is a read-only operation that does not change the chain and often returns immediately. For example, api. query. system. account returns account balances and nonce information. Use api. tx when you intend to change state: this constructs an extrinsic that must be signed and sent. For example, api. tx. balances. transfer creates a transfer extrinsic. Subscriptions are a third pattern: when you need to react to on-chain events as they happen, subscribe to api. query. system. events or use subscriptions on specific storage items to get push updates. Subscriptions are more efficient than polling and essential for live UIs that must react to new blocks or transfer events. A misconception is that api. query can notify you of future changes; it cannot unless you subscribe. Also remember an extrinsic broadcast returns a hash but not a guarantee of finalization; use status callbacks to observe inclusion and finality. Choosing the right method matters for UX, resource usage, and correctness.

Security is central when interacting with a blockchain that holds value. First, private keys must never be exposed in plaintext or committed to version control. Second, be cautious about RPC endpoints: a malicious or compromised node can return incorrect state or censor transactions. Always verify the origin of public RPCs and prefer connecting to nodes you control when testing critical functionality. Third, review transactions before signing: confirm recipient addresses, amounts, and call parameters. Also, recognize the risk of replay or incorrect nonce handling if you reuse keypairs across multiple concurrent scripts. Subscriptions let your application react to on-chain events without polling. With Polkadot-JS A P I you can subscribe to api. query. system. events to receive a stream of events emitted in each block, or subscribe to specific storage items to get updates when they change. Use event subscriptions to filter for particular pallet events such as transfer events or custom pallet notifications. Moving from development to production requires deliberate changes. Replace development key URIs with secure signing flows such as hardware wallets or remote signing services. Prefer connecting to trusted node endpoints under your control or to audited public endpoints to reduce risk of data tampering. Add extensive logging around signAndSend and subscription handlers so you can trace transaction lifecycles and handle retries or nonce mismatches. For testing, use a dedicated testnet or local node and reproduce the exact steps your production flow will take. When loading runtime metadata, cache it when appropriate but refresh metadata if you upgrade your runtime to avoid encoding mismatches. Let's summarize the most important terms from this chapter. RPC is the transport that carries method calls and responses between clients and a Substrate node.
